newsitem.title: UK: Amersham poised for drug discovery explosion.
newsitem.headline: Amersham poised for drug discovery explosion.

text.p: British healthcare and technology group Amersham International Plc said on Monday that its fast-growing drug discovery business was poised to take advantage of an explosion in drug development based on gene therapy.

In an interview with Reuters, chief executive Bill Castell said that the growing understanding of how human genes function "is more important than the discovery of hygiene in what it can do for the quality of life...it will change the way we diagnose disease, control disease and treat disease."

Since taking control of Amersham in 1990 Castell has pushed the group's Life Sciences division towards the high growth area of drug discovery technology to offset the decline of its mature radioactive chemicals business.

Earlier on Monday Amersham won two Queen's Awards for technological achievement for equipment capable of rapid screening of tens of thousands of potential drug molecules. The SPA and Cytostar-T systems are used by virtually all leading international drug companies.

"In the mid-1980s the pharmaceutical industry was screening about 10,000 compounds a year, and now it is screening about 10,000 a day," said Castell, who said the industry was at the point of going from feast to famine in terms of innovative new products.

One of Amersham's prize-winning drug assay systems, SPA, can tell at high speed how well a drug molecule will bind to its chosen target in the body, or conversely if it will prevent molecules from binding together. Amersham said most of the world's top 30 drug companies were using SPA in programmes for inflammation, cancer, rheumatoid arthritis, heart disease and asthma. The system is also used extensively in AIDS drug research.

Britain's Zeneca Group Plc , a major user of the system, told Reuters that SPA "has been one of the most significant assay technology advances in recent years and has had a great impact on high throughput screening."

Where SPA can measure what impact chemicals have had on a cell which is effectively dead, Cytostar-T enables scientists to monitor the impact on living cells, measuring their reaction over time. "That's unique to Amersham," said Castell.
Castell, who joined Amersham from Wellcome Plc , made the development of drug screening technology a priority when he took over, and the strategy is now bearing fruit.

In January the company said turnover of non-radioactive products including drug screening had for the first time overtaken sales of radioactive chemicals, an expertise derived from Amersham's origins as a secret government research base in World War II.
Castell predicted further strong growth in drug discovery technology, helping to lift the core Life Sciences business after several flat years.

Amersham, building on traditional strengths in radiochemical labelling, also has products for labelling and detecting DNA, the molecules which form the body's chemical building blocks, and for tracking the sequences that makes up each type of DNA and the chemical reactions within the body.

Castell said the 250 million stg annual market for gene-related drug discovery is growing at 20 percent a year, and predicted that in the next five to 10 years it would be worth more than 1 billion stg.

With the international project to map the whole of the human genome, working out the sequence of all three billion building blocks of human DNA, making rapid progress, Castell said the drugs industry was preparing to move into a period of "immense productivity' after a decade of falling output of new drugs.
"We are well-positioned to be a good competitor in this field," he said.
